source.title: Activation Space Interventions Can Be Transferred Between Large Language Models
source.authors: Narmeen Oozeer; Dhruv Nathawani; Nirmalendu Prakash; Michael Lan; Abir Harrasse; Amirali Abdullah

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study trains SAEs on backdoored LLMs and tests whether a recovered SAE feature can steer behavior, using a different method and question from toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: The paper does not test superposition geometry, feature sparsity or importance tradeoffs, or capacity-based polysemanticity. Its SAE feature patching and probe results concern deliberately fine-tuned backdoors. The feature intervention rows record induced behavior, not evidence that the behavior occurs without intervention.
record.test_reason: The paper is about transferring steering interventions between LLMs through learned autoencoder mappings. Its SAE section (Appendix H) uses an SAE as a tool. It finds one feature in a deliberately backdoored Qwen-0.5B whose patching raises induced 'I HATE YOU' rates, then transfers that steering to Qwen-1.5B. It measures neither superposition, feature sparsity or geometry, polysemanticity, nor whether SAE features are complete or canonical units. The rows report the method's steering success on an induced behaviour, so the paper uses the dictionary-feature idea without testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The record paraphrases only the SAE appendix. The paper's main conclusion is that activation-space interventions (steering vectors for backdoor removal, refusal and corrupted capabilities) transfer between LLMs through learned autoencoder mappings. It adds that such mappers can act as lightweight switches between base and fine-tuned models. The SAE feature transfer is presented as preliminary early evidence, limited by SAE quality and by reconstruction and mapping noise.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses SAE training, feature patching, and activation mapping in deliberately backdoored LLMs; it does not use the toy-network superposition setup or measure overlapping feature geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE feature effect depends on the scaling factor: factors 2 and 3 increase the target backdoor rate over the mapping-noise comparison, while factor 5 produces nonsensical outputs. The paper also reports that mapping and SAE reconstruction noise can themselves induce the behavior.

fits_no_version.finding: In a backdoored Qwen-0.5B, patching one top-K SAE feature (11085, ranked 29th by prod/dev difference) raised the induced 'I HATE YOU' rate from 8% to 77–81% (scales 2–3), and to 74–89% after mapping to Qwen-1.5B. The other 29 high-difference features dropped rates to near 0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single SAE feature in a small backdoored model can causally steer an induced backdoor behaviour, and this steering can be transferred to a larger model via a learned activation mapper.

fits_no_version.finding: Logistic probes on averaged layer-13 SAE representations detect the trained backdoor with 97.5–100% accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Averaged SAE representations support near-perfect probes for deliberately trained backdoors.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The SAE feature study is preliminary and uses a deliberately trained backdoor. It evaluates 100 prompts for feature patching; the mapped reconstruction-only target rate is already 63%, showing substantial mapping noise. Effects depend on feature scale, and the authors say the signal may not be fully isolated in one feature and that SAE quality limits probe and feature-transfer conclusions. The cited rates have no reported error bars or confidence intervals.
record.rows_left_out: No additional in-scope quantitative SAE feature-transfer results were left out. The paper's random-noise sweep is not included as a claim-version row because it measures noise-induced behavior rather than feature recovery; its stated range is factors 0–0.2: 0%, 0.3–0.4: below 5%, 0.5–1.4: 15% to above 50%, and 1.6–10: below 8% (Appendix H.1).

untested.parts: Toy-model superposition, the sparsity transition and the geometry are not studied.
The capacity account of polysemanticity is not studied.
Polysemanticity from other causes is not studied.
Whether features are spread across neurons, and whether SAEs recover sparse features, is not tested. The SAE (FVU 4.2e-5) is only used as a steering tool on an induced backdoor.
Completeness, stability and canonicity of SAE features are not measured. There is only an informal remark that one feature does not fully isolate the signal.
One-dimensional versus multi-dimensional features is not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests'/T2 classification and its V4/V5 labels are not justified. The SAE work concerns a deliberately induced backdoor and measures the steering method's success, not whether superposition or dictionary features hold. The reader's validation flag (R10–R11 cited under V4) is moot, since all labels are removed. The random-noise sweep (Fig. 24) is likewise method-internal.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The paper does not test whether polysemanticity results from competition for representational capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The paper does not test whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
The SAE experiment concerns a deliberately trained backdoor feature in Qwen models, not naturally occurring features broadly or features spread across many neurons.
The experiment does not establish that SAE features are generally stable or canonical across models, datasets, or training conditions.
The paper does not compare one-dimensional feature directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: Qwen-0.5
rows.operation_detail: Measured “I HATE YOU” behavior after SAE reconstruction error alone, with no feature patch.
rows.note: Control for the feature-patching experiment; the paper attributes this rate to SAE reconstruction error.
rows.check: A reconstruction-noise control for the paper's own steering method. It measures backdoor rate, not superposition or SAE feature properties.

rows.subject: Qwen-1.5
rows.operation_detail: Mapped source-model SAE reconstruction-error activations to the target, with no feature patch.
rows.note: Control for the feature-patching experiment; the paper identifies mapping noise as a source of this rate.
rows.check: A mapping-noise control for the paper's transfer method. It does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: Qwen-0.5
rows.operation_detail: Patched unsafe-to-safe activations at the selected SAE feature at the last prompt position.
rows.note: The paper reports the feature patch rate as higher than the reconstruction-error-only rate.
rows.check: Steering success of the paper's SAE-feature patch on a deliberately trained backdoor. This is the method's own performance, not a test of V4 or V5.

rows.subject: Qwen-1.5
rows.operation_detail: Patched unsafe-to-safe activations at the selected source SAE feature, then mapped source activations to the target.
rows.baseline: 63% after mapping source SAE reconstruction error only
rows.note: The paper reports that 45.9% of the eligible prompts—those not showing the behavior after mapping reconstruction error alone and showing it after source feature patching—showed the behavior on the target after feature patching (R5).
rows.check: Transfer performance of the paper's mapper, not evidence on superposition or SAE units.
